claim: Schwann cells express Hdac4, 5, and 7 but not Hdac9.
source: Of this family, Schwann cells express Hdac4, 5, and 7 but not Hdac9.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is supported by experimental data shown in the manuscript.

claim: When Hdac4 and 5 are knocked-out from Schwann cells in mice, a JUN-dependent mechanism induces the compensatory overexpression of Hdac7.
source: Thus, when Hdac4 and 5 are knocked-out from Schwann cells in mice, a JUN-dependent mechanism induces the compensatory overexpression of Hdac7 permitting, although with a delay, the formation of the myelin sheath.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data including RT-qPCR, ChIP-qPCR, and luciferase assays shown in the manuscript.

claim: Hdac7 overexpression permits myelin sheath formation with a delay in Hdac4/5 double knockout mice.
source: Thus, when Hdac4 and 5 are knocked-out from Schwann cells in mice, a JUN-dependent mechanism induces the compensatory overexpression of Hdac7 permitting, although with a delay, the formation of the myelin sheath.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by morphological analysis and gene expression data.

claim: When Hdac4, 5, and 7 are simultaneously removed, MEF2D binds to the promoter and induces the de novo expression of Hdac9.
source: When Hdac4, 5, and 7 are simultaneously removed, the myocyte-specific enhancer-factor d (MEF2D) binds to the promoter and induces the de novo expression of Hdac9
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by ChIP-qPCR, Western blot, and RNA-seq data.

claim: In triple knockout mice (Hdac4/5/7), several melanocytic lineage genes are misexpressed.
source: When Hdac4, 5, and 7 are simultaneously removed, the myocyte-specific enhancer-factor d (MEF2D) binds to the promoter and induces the de novo expression of Hdac9, and although several melanocytic lineage genes are misexpressed and Remak bundle structure is disrupted, myelination proceeds after a long delay.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by RNA-seq, RT-qPCR, Western blot, and immunofluorescence data.

claim: Remak bundle structure is disrupted in triple knockout mice.
source: When Hdac4, 5, and 7 are simultaneously removed, the myocyte-specific enhancer-factor d (MEF2D) binds to the promoter and induces the de novo expression of Hdac9, and although several melanocytic lineage genes are misexpressed and Remak bundle structure is disrupted, myelination proceeds after a long delay.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by electron microscopy data showing altered axon segregation.

claim: Myelination proceeds after a long delay in triple knockout mice.
source: When Hdac4, 5, and 7 are simultaneously removed, the myocyte-specific enhancer-factor d (MEF2D) binds to the promoter and induces the de novo expression of Hdac9, and although several melanocytic lineage genes are misexpressed and Remak bundle structure is disrupted, myelination proceeds after a long delay.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by morphological analysis at multiple developmental time points.

claim: The compensatory mechanism within the class IIa Hdac family guarantees the ability of Schwann cells to myelinate during development.
source: Thus, our data unveil a finely tuned compensatory mechanism within the class IIa Hdac family, coordinated by distinct transcription factors, that guarantees the ability of Schwann cells to myelinate during development and remyelinate after nerve injury.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The compensatory mechanism within the class IIa Hdac family guarantees the ability of Schwann cells to remyelinate after nerve injury.
source: Thus, our data unveil a finely tuned compensatory mechanism within the class IIa Hdac family, coordinated by distinct transcription factors, that guarantees the ability of Schwann cells to myelinate during development and remyelinate after nerve injury.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a conclusion drawn from nerve injury experiments.

claim: Immature Schwann cells downregulate the transcription factor Jun during postnatal development.

evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Jun negatively regulates myelination.
source: Immature Schwann cells downregulate the transcription factor Jun (which negatively regulates myelination) and upregulate the expression of transcriptional regulators of myelination such as Krox-20 and Yy1 (Fazal et al., 2017; Monk et al., 2015; Parkinson et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated explicitly in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Immature Schwann cells upregulate the expression of Krox-20 and Yy1 during postnatal development.
source: Immature Schwann cells downregulate the transcription factor Jun (which negatively regulates myelination) and upregulate the expression of transcriptional regulators of myelination such as Krox-20 and Yy1 (Fazal et al., 2017; Monk et al., 2015; Parkinson et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Krox-20 and Yy1 are transcriptional regulators of myelination.

evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Jun is strongly reexpressed after nerve injury.
source: Jun is strongly reexpressed after nerve injury enabling trans-differentiation of Schwann cells into a repair phenotype that promotes axon regeneration and functional nerve repair (Arthur-Farraj et al., 2012; Gomez-Sanchez et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Jun reexpression enables trans-differentiation of Schwann cells into a repair phenotype that promotes axon regeneration and functional nerve repair.
source: Jun is strongly reexpressed after nerve injury enabling trans-differentiation of Schwann cells into a repair phenotype that promotes axon regeneration and functional nerve repair (Arthur-Farraj et al., 2012; Gomez-Sanchez et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: After axon regeneration, Schwann cells reestablish contact with axons and downregulate Jun.
source: After axon regeneration Schwann cells reestablish contact with them and downregulate Jun.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is consistent with established knowledge in the field.

claim: Jun downregulation allows reexpression of Krox-20 and reactivation of a gene expression program aimed at remyelination.
source: This allows reexpression of Krox-20 and the consequent reactivation of a gene expression program aimed at remyelination of axons and reestablishment of nerve function (Stassart and Woodhoo, 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: Activation of Gpr126 is required for Schwann cell myelination and remyelination.

claim: Gpr126 is a G-protein-coupled receptor that increases intracellular levels of cAMP.
source: Activation of Gpr126, a G-protein-coupled receptor that increases intracellular levels of cAMP, is required for Schwann cell myelination and remyelination (Monk et al., 2009; Monk et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: The prodifferentiating activity of cAMP is in part mediated by its ability to shuttle HDAC4 into the nucleus of Schwann cells.
source: We have recently shown that the prodifferentiating activity of cAMP is in part mediated by its ability to shuttle HDAC4 into the nucleus of Schwann cells (Gomis-Coloma et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: Nuclear HDAC4 recruits the complex NcoR1/HDAC3 and deacetylates histone three on the promoter of Jun, repressing its expression.
source: Nuclear HDAC4 recruits the complex NcoR1/HDAC3 and deacetylates histone three on the promoter of Jun, repressing its expression.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is based on the authors' previous work.

claim: HDAC4 promotes Krox-20 expression and activation of the myelination program.
source: At the same time HDAC4 promotes Krox-20 expression and activation of the myelination program (Velasco-Aviles et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: Hdac5 is able to partially compensate for the loss of Hdac4 expression in Schwann cells in vivo.

claim: There is an additional compensatory mechanism permitting nerve myelination in Hdac4/5 double knockout mice.

claim: The expression of Hdac7 was substantially induced in the sciatic nerve of the dKO mice at P60 (325.1 ± 48.1%; p = 0.0034, n = 4).

claim: Hdac9 expression remained residual in the sciatic nerve of the dKO mice at P60.

claim: Hdac7 overexpression is specific for the dKO, as minor or no changes at all were found in the single KOs.
source: This is specific for the dKO, as minor or no changes at all were found in the single KOs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B).

claim: Hdac7 overexpression can be detected early during development.
source: Importantly, Hdac7 overexpression can be detected early during development (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).

claim: The simultaneous elimination of Hdac4 and Hdac5 from Schwann cells activates a mechanism aimed to compensate for the drop in the gene dose of class IIa Hdacs that upregulates threefold the expression of Hdac7.
source: These results suggest that the simultaneous elimination of Hdac4 and Hdac5 from Schwann cells activates a mechanism aimed to compensate for the drop in the gene dose of class IIa Hdacs that upregulates threefold the expression of Hdac7.

claim: The simultaneous elimination of Hdac4, 5, and 7 from Schwann cells produced a much more pronounced delay in myelin development.
source: Strikingly, the simultaneous elimination of Hdac4, 5, and 7 from Schwann cells produced a much more pronounced delay in myelin development (Figure 1B–J).

claim: Expression of negative regulators of myelination (including Jun) was notably increased from P2 to P21 in tKO mice.
source: Interestingly, expression of the negative regulators of myelination (including Jun) was notably increased from P2 to P21, which can explain the delay in the expression of myelin genes (Figure 1K–M) and in morphological parameters of myelin development in the tKO mice.

claim: Hdac7 upregulation can compensate for the absence of Hdac4 and Hdac5 allowing myelination to proceed, although with some delay.
source: Thus, our data demonstrate that Hdac7 upregulation can compensate for the absence of Hdac4 and Hdac5 allowing myelination to proceed, although with some delay.

claim: Adult tKO nerves show almost normal myelination parameters.
source: Interestingly, and although the coordinated removal of Hdac4, Hdac5, and Hdac7 produces a long delay in myelination, myelin is finally formed and adult tKO nerves show almost normal myelination parameters (Figure 2A–D).

claim: Remak bundles are profoundly altered in adult tKO nerves, with many axons not properly segregated.
source: Despite PNS myelination looks normal in the adult (p60) tKO mice, we found the Remak bundles profoundly altered in these nerves, with many axons not properly segregated (Figure 2E).

claim: There is a significant increase in the number of pockets with two to five axons in tKO Remak bundles.
source: Thus, there is a significant increase in the number of pockets with two to five axons and, although it is very rare to find pockets with more than five axons in the control (2.3%), an important number of axons are grouped together in packs of more than five in the tKO (16.5%), with some of them being in pockets of more than 30 axons.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by morphometric analysis of electron microscopy data.

claim: In tKO nerves, 16.5% of axons are grouped together in packs of more than five, with some in pockets of more than 30 axons.
source: Thus, there is a significant increase in the number of pockets with two to five axons and, although it is very rare to find pockets with more than five axons in the control (2.3%), an important number of axons are grouped together in packs of more than five in the tKO (16.5%), with some of them being in pockets of more than 30 axons.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by morphometric analysis.

claim: No major changes in Remak bundle structure were observed in single KO or dKO nerves.
source: These defects are specific of the tKO, as no major changes were observed in the single neither the dKO nerves (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).

source: Surprisingly, the most robustly upregulated gene is the tyrosinase-related protein one encoding gene (Tyrp1; Log FC = 6.03; FDR = 0), a melanocyte lineage-specific gene (Figure 2G, H).
evidence: This is stated in the results and is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Mcam and Ngfr genes are highly induced in the sciatic nerves of the tKO.

claim: The expression of Mitf and Ednrb increased in tKO nerves.

source: Thus, our data suggest that class IIa HDACs are necessary to allow Schwann cell precursors (SCPs) to differentiate into Remak Schwann cells and properly segregate small size axons.

claim: The increased number of Schwann cells in tKO nerves is probably consequence of over-proliferation.
source: The increased number of Schwann cells is probably consequence of over-proliferation, as suggested by Ki67 staining (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the results as an interpretation supported by Ki67 staining data.

claim: A decrease in the number of axons >1.5 μm was observed at 20 and 30 dpi in tKO nerves, probably because of the smaller diameter of the unmyelinated axons.
source: We also observed a decrease in the number of axons >1.5 μm at 20 and 30 dpi (Figure 5J), probably because the smaller diameter of the unmyelinated axons.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by morphological data shown in Figure 5J.

claim: JUN protein is clearly more abundant in the nerves of the tKO than in either control littermates or wild-types, both at 10 and 21 dpi.
source: As shown in Figure 5O, JUN protein is clearly more abundant in the nerves of the tKO than in either control littermates or wild-types, both at 10 and 21 dpi.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5O.

claim: The amount of MPZ protein is lower at 10 and 21 dpi in tKO nerves.
source: Conversely, the amount of MPZ protein is lower at 10 and 21 dpi.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Western blot data.

claim: KROX-20 is lower at 10 dpi in the tKO, but levels had recovered by 21 dpi.
source: KROX-20 is also lower at 10 dpi in the tKO, but levels had recovered by 21 dpi.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Western blot data.

claim: No differences in voltage amplitude or nerve conduction velocity (NCV) were found between tKO and controls in uninjured nerves.
source: In uninjured nerves, we found no differences in voltage amplitude or nerve conduction velocity (NCV) between tKO and controls (Figure 6A–D)
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 6A-D.

claim: At 40 dpi, six of nine sciatic nerves of control mice showed a response when electrically stimulated at 8 V, while only one of eight tKO responded.
source: By contrast, at 40 dpi, whereas six of nine sciatic nerves of control mice showed a response when electrically stimulated at 8 V, only one of eight tKO responded (Figure 6E, F).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 6E and 6F.

claim: At 40 dpi and 15 V stimulation, eight of nine control mice responded while only four of eight tKO responded.
source: At 15 V, eight of nine control mice responded while only four of eight tKO responded.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by electrophysiological data.

claim: The amplitude of the A-fiber component of the compound action potential (CAP) was decreased for 8, 10, and 15 V stimuli at 40 dpi in tKO nerves.
source: In the same line, the amplitude of the A-fiber component of the compound action potential (CAP) was decreased for 8, 10, and 15 V stimuli (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: The amplitude of the C-fiber component was decreased for 8 and 10 V stimulation at 40 dpi in tKO nerves.
source: Regarding the component corresponding to C fibers, amplitude was also decreased for 8 and 10 V stimulation (Figure 6H).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 6H.

claim: NCV showed a statistically significant decrease when using 15 V stimuli at 40 dpi in tKO nerves.
source: Moreover, NCV showed a statistically significant decrease when using 15 V stimuli (Figure 6I).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 6I.

claim: The kinetics of remyelination after nerve injury is directly correlated with class IIa Hdac gene dose.
source: All together our data demonstrate that the kinetics of remyelination after nerve injury is directly correlated with class IIa Hdac gene dose.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: At 1 dpi, 395 genes were upregulated and 274 downregulated in the tKO.
source: At 1 dpi, 395 genes were upregulated and 274 downregulated in the tKO (Figure 5—figure supplement 4A and Figure 5—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by RNA-seq data in supplementary figures.

claim: The 10 most robustly changed genes at 1 dpi were all upregulated.
source: Similar to the uninjured nerve analysis, the 10 most robustly changed genes were all upregulated.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: Tyrp1 and Mcam were among the most upregulated genes at 1 dpi in tKO nerves.
source: Interestingly, Tyrp1 and Mcam were also among the most upregulated genes.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: At 10 dpi, 1227 transcripts were upregulated and 1550 downregulated in tKO nerves.
source: At 10 dpi, the number of dysregulated genes was notably increased, with 1227 transcripts upregulated and 1550 downregulated (Figure 5—figure supplement 4B and Figure 5—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by RNA-seq data in supplementary figures.

claim: Bdnf was among the most robustly upregulated genes at 10 dpi in tKO nerves.
source: Among the most robustly upregulated genes were the repair cell marker Bdnf (Arthur-Farraj et al., 2017; Jessen and Mirsky, 2019), possibly reflecting impairment of the tKO repair Schwann cells to fully redifferentiate into myelin and nonmyelin-forming Schwann cells.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by RNA-seq data and citations.

claim: At 10 dpi, 8 of the 10 most robustly changed genes were downregulated, including many myelin-related genes (Mal, Prx, Mag, Ncmap, Pmp22, Mbp, and Mpz).
source: Interestingly, in contrast with previous time points, 8 of the 10 most robustly changed genes were downregulated, including many myelin-related genes (Mal, Prx, Mag, Ncmap, Pmp22, Mbp, and Mpz), which is expected given the dramatic delay in myelin sheath development in the tKO at 10 dpi (Figure 5N).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: At 20 dpi, 1895 transcripts were upregulated and 2450 downregulated in the tKO.
source: At 20 dpi, we identified 1895 transcripts upregulated and 2450 downregulated in the tKO (Figure 5—figure supplement 4C and Figure 5—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by RNA-seq data in supplementary figures.

claim: The 10 most robustly changed genes at 20 dpi were upregulated and among them were Tyrp1, Mcam, and Ednrb.
source: As before, the 10 most robustly changed genes were upregulated and among them we found again Tyrp1, Mcam, and Ednrb (Figure 5—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by RNA-seq data in supplementary figures.

claim: Jun was upregulated in the tKO from 1 dpi and remained increased up to 20 dpi.
source: The negative regulator of myelination Jun was upregulated in the tKO from 1 dpi and remained increased up to 20 dpi (Figure 5—figure supplement 5B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by RNA-seq data in supplementary figures.

claim: Runx2, Gdnf, Ngfr, and Sox2 showed a similar upregulation profile to Jun in tKO nerves.
source: A similar profile was shown for Runx2, Gdnf, Ngfr, and Sox2 (Figure 5—figure supplement 5C–F).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by RNA-seq data in supplementary figures.

claim: Pou3f1 was induced up to 10 dpi in both control and tKO nerves, to later (20 dpi) be downregulated in the control but not in the tKO nerves.
source: Pou3f1 was induced up to 10 dpi in both control and tKO nerves, to later (20 dpi) be downregulated in the control (20 dpi) but not in the tKO nerves (Figure 5—figure supplement 5G).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by RNA-seq data in supplementary figures.

claim: Krox-20 was downregulated at 10 and 20 dpi in the tKO, when remyelination was highly active in the controls.
source: By contrast, the master transcriptional regulator of myelination Krox-20 was downregulated at 10 and 20 dpi in the tKO, when remyelination was highly active in the controls (Figure 5—figure supplement 5H).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by RNA-seq data in supplementary figures.

claim: Early myelin genes such as Drp2 and Prx were downregulated in tKO nerves.
source: Probably as a consequence, early myelin genes such as Drp2 and Prx were downregulated (Figure 5—figure supplement 5I, J).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by RNA-seq data in supplementary figures.

claim: Myelin protein genes Mpz, Mbp, Mag, Pmp22, and Plp1 were consistently downregulated in tKO nerves.
source: Other myelin protein genes that are expressed later, such as Mpz, Mbp, Mag, Pmp22, and Plp1 were also consistently downregulated (Figure 5—figure supplement 5K–O).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by RNA-seq data in supplementary figures.

claim: Several genes of the sterol branch of the mevalonate pathway (Hmgcs, Lss, and Dhcr24) were downregulated during remyelination of the tKO nerves.
source: During remyelination of the tKO nerves we found several genes of the sterol branch of the mevalonate pathway downregulated (Hmgcs, Lss, and Dhcr24) (Figure 5—figure supplement 5P–R).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by RNA-seq data in supplementary figures.

claim: Genes encoding for enzymes involved in the elongation (Elovl1), transport (Pmp2) and insertion of double bonds (Scd2 and Fads1) into fatty acids were downregulated in tKO nerves.
source: We also found downregulated genes encoding for enzymes involved in the elongation (Elovl1), transport (Pmp2) and insertion of double bonds (Scd2 and Fads1) into fatty acids (Figure 5—figure supplement 5S–V).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by RNA-seq data in supplementary figures.

claim: Cers2 and Ugt8a were downregulated in tKO nerves.
source: Interestingly, Cers2 and Ugt8a were also downregulated.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: Cers2 and Ugt8a are involved in the synthesis of sphingomyelin and galactosyl-ceramide, respectively.
source: These genes are involved in the synthesis of sphingomyelin and galactosyl-ceramide, respectively (Figure 5—figure supplement 5W, X), both abundant lipids in myelin (Poitelon et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by a citation.

claim: Class IIa HDACs are necessary to block negative regulators of myelination and induce the expression of genes encoding for myelin proteins and key enzymes for the biosynthesis of myelin lipids.
source: Together our data show that class IIa HDACs are necessary to block negative regulators of myelination and induce the expression of genes encoding for myelin proteins and key enzymes for the biosynthesis of myelin lipids.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a conclusion drawn from the RNA-seq data.

claim: 3,932 peaks were found in the ChIP-Seq analysis of HDAC4 in dbcAMP differentiated Schwann cells.
source: We found 3.932 peaks, 67.27% of which were located in the proximal promoter regions of genes (≤1 kb from the transcription start site [TSS]) (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by ChIP-Seq data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: 67.27% of HDAC4 ChIP-Seq peaks were located in the proximal promoter regions of genes (≤1 kb from the TSS).
source: We found 3.932 peaks, 67.27% of which were located in the proximal promoter regions of genes (≤1 kb from the transcription start site [TSS]) (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by ChIP-Seq data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: ChIP-Seq analysis confirmed that HDAC4 binds to the promoters of Jun, Gdnf, and Runx2.
source: Importantly, ChIP-Seq analysis confirmed our previous results (Gomis-Coloma et al., 2018) showing that HDAC4 binds to the promoters of Jun, Gdnf, and Runx2 (Figure 7B–E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by ChIP-Seq data shown in Figure 7B-E and a citation to previous work.

claim: HDAC4 binds to the promoter region of Sox2.
source: Interestingly, HDAC4 also binds to the promoter region of Sox2 (Figure 7B, F), another negative regulator of myelination.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by ChIP-Seq data shown in Figure 7B and 7F.

claim: Sox2 is a negative regulator of myelination.
source: Interestingly, HDAC4 also binds to the promoter region of Sox2 (Figure 7B, F), another negative regulator of myelination.
evidence: This is stated in the results and is consistent with established knowledge in the field.

claim: Peaks for Id2 and Hey2 were found in the HDAC4 ChIP-Seq.
source: We found also peaks for Id2 and Hey2 (Figure 7B) and source data file three online (ChIP-Seq peaks source data).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by ChIP-Seq data shown in Figure 7B and source data files.

claim: Pou3f1 is overexpressed in the PNS of the tKO during development.
source: Here, we show that Pou3f1 is overexpressed in the PNS of the tKO during development (Figure 1K–M), and that it is not properly downregulated during remyelination (Figure 5—figure supplement 5G).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1K-M and supplementary figures.

claim: Pou3f1 is not properly downregulated during remyelination in tKO nerves.
source: Here, we show that Pou3f1 is overexpressed in the PNS of the tKO during development (Figure 1K–M), and that it is not properly downregulated during remyelination (Figure 5—figure supplement 5G).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by RNA-seq data in supplementary figures.

claim: Three peaks of HDAC4 were found bound near the TSS of Pou3f1.
source: Interestingly, we found three peaks of HDAC4 bound near the TSS of Pou3f1 (Figure 7B–G), a result that was confirmed by ChIP-qPCR (Figure 7H).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by ChIP-Seq data shown in Figure 7B-G.

claim: HDAC4 binding to the Pou3f1 promoter was confirmed by ChIP-qPCR.
source: Interestingly, we found three peaks of HDAC4 bound near the TSS of Pou3f1 (Figure 7B–G), a result that was confirmed by ChIP-qPCR (Figure 7H).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 7H.

claim: A clear peak of HDAC4 was found close to the TSS of Mcam.
source: Regarding the melanocyte lineage, we found a clear peak of HDAC4 close the TSS of Mcam (Figure 7B), however, we did not detect peaks in Tyrp1 and Ednrb, suggesting that, while HDAC4 directly represses the expression of Mcam it likely indirectly leads to Tyrp1 and Ednrb repression.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by ChIP-Seq data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: No peaks were detected for Tyrp1 and Ednrb in the HDAC4 ChIP-Seq.
source: Regarding the melanocyte lineage, we found a clear peak of HDAC4 close the TSS of Mcam (Figure 7B), however, we did not detect peaks in Tyrp1 and Ednrb, suggesting that, while HDAC4 directly represses the expression of Mcam it likely indirectly leads to Tyrp1 and Ednrb repression.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by ChIP-Seq data.

claim: HDAC4 directly represses the expression of Mcam.
source: Regarding the melanocyte lineage, we found a clear peak of HDAC4 close the TSS of Mcam (Figure 7B), however, we did not detect peaks in Tyrp1 and Ednrb, suggesting that, while HDAC4 directly represses the expression of Mcam it likely indirectly leads to Tyrp1 and Ednrb repression.
evidence: This is stated in the results as an interpretation of the ChIP-Seq data.

claim: HDAC4 likely indirectly leads to Tyrp1 and Ednrb repression.
source: Regarding the melanocyte lineage, we found a clear peak of HDAC4 close the TSS of Mcam (Figure 7B), however, we did not detect peaks in Tyrp1 and Ednrb, suggesting that, while HDAC4 directly represses the expression of Mcam it likely indirectly leads to Tyrp1 and Ednrb repression.
evidence: This is stated in the results as an interpretation of the ChIP-Seq data.

claim: Peaks were found in the promoter regions of Mbp and Hmgcr in the HDAC4 ChIP-Seq.
source: Surprisingly, we also found peaks in the promoter regions of Mbp and Hmgcr (Figure 7B), two genes highly expressed during myelination.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by ChIP-Seq data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Mbp and Hmgcr are highly expressed during myelination.
source: Surprisingly, we also found peaks in the promoter regions of Mbp and Hmgcr (Figure 7B), two genes highly expressed during myelination.
evidence: This is stated in the results and is consistent with established knowledge in the field.

claim: HDACs have been shown to be bound to the promoter regions of highly expressed genes in other tissues.
source: Although it could seem contradictory as HDACs have mainly been described as transcriptional repressors, HDACs have been shown to be bound to the promoter regions of highly expressed genes in other tissues (Wang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Jun is highly expressed in the developing PNS of the dKO mice.
source: We have shown before that Jun is highly expressed in the developing PNS of the dKO mice (Gomis-Coloma et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by a citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: Jun expression remains high during remyelination in the dKO sciatic nerves.
source: Here, we show that Jun expression remains high during remyelination in the dKO sciatic nerves (Figure 4L, N and Figure 5—figure supplement 5B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by RT-qPCR and RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4L, 4N, and supplementary figures.

claim: JUN binds to the promoter region of Hdac7 in A549 cells.
source: Interestingly, we found in ENCODE (https://www.encodeproject.org/) that JUN binds to the promoter region of Hdac7 in A549 cells.
evidence: This is stated in the results and is based on data from the ENCODE database.

claim: In cultured Schwann cells, JUN binds to the Hdac7 promoter.
source: To test this, we used ChIP-qPCR and found that, indeed, in cultured Schwann cells JUN binds to the Hdac7 promoter (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: An evolutionarily conserved JUN consensus binding motif was identified in the proximal promoter region of the mouse Hdac7 gene.
source: We then identified an evolutionarily conserved JUN consensus binding motif in the proximal promoter region of the mouse Hdac7 gene (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by sequence alignment data in supplementary figures.

claim: The Hdac7 promoter fragment responded to JUN by increasing the luciferase activity by 3.4-fold over the control.
source: As shown in Figure 8B, this promoter fragment responded to JUN by increasing the luciferase activity by 3.4-fold over the control, which supports the idea that Hdac7 expression is regulated by JUN.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Jun overexpression in Schwann cells induced Hdac7 expression by almost twofold.
source: Jun overexpression in Schwann cells induced Hdac7 expression by almost twofold (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Jun overexpression had no effect on Hdac4 and Hdac5 mRNA levels.
source: This was a specific effect as no changes were found for Hdac4 and Hdac5 mRNA (Figure 8E, F).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 8E and 8F.

claim: Jun removal produced no changes in the expression of any class IIa Hdacs.
source: By contrast, Jun removal produced no changes in the expression of any class IIa Hdacs, suggesting it is not necessary for the basal expression of these Hdacs (Figure 8D–F).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 8D-F.

claim: Jun is not necessary for the basal expression of class IIa Hdacs.
source: By contrast, Jun removal produced no changes in the expression of any class IIa Hdacs, suggesting it is not necessary for the basal expression of these Hdacs (Figure 8D–F).
evidence: This is stated in the results as an interpretation of the RT-qPCR data.

claim: JUN induces the expression of Hdac7 by Schwann cells in vivo.
source: Thus, our data clearly show that JUN induces the expression of Hdac7 by Schwann cells in vivo.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Hdac7 is not overexpressed in the nerves of the dKO that lack Jun in Schwann cells (dKO;Jun_cKO).
source: Further supporting this tenet, we found that Hdac7 is not overexpressed in the nerves of the dKO that lack Jun in Schwann cells (dKO;Jun_cKO) (Figure 8G).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 8G.

claim: A peak of HDAC4 was detected bound to the promoter of Hdac7 in the ChIP-Seq experiment.
source: Interestingly, we detected a peak of HDAC4 bound to the promoter of Hdac7 (Figures 7B and 8H) in the ChIP-Seq experiment, a result that we confirmed by ChIP-qPCR (Figure 8I).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by ChIP-Seq data shown in Figures 7B and 8H.

claim: HDAC4 binding to the Hdac7 promoter was confirmed by ChIP-qPCR.
source: Interestingly, we detected a peak of HDAC4 bound to the promoter of Hdac7 (Figures 7B and 8H) in the ChIP-Seq experiment, a result that we confirmed by ChIP-qPCR (Figure 8I).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 8I.

claim: In differentiated Schwann cells, other class IIa HDACs contribute to maintaining Hdac7 expression at the basal level.
source: This suggests that, in differentiated Schwann cells, other class IIa HDACs contribute to maintaining Hdac7 expression at the basal level.
evidence: This is stated in the results as an interpretation of the ChIP-Seq and ChIP-qPCR data.

claim: The simultaneous loss of Hdac4 and Hdac5 allows the expression of Jun, which can bind to the promoter of Hdac7, now free of the repression by class IIa HDACs, increasing the transcription of this deacetylase.
source: The simultaneous loss of Hdac4 and Hdac5 allows the expression of Jun, which can bind to the promoter of Hdac7, now free of the repression by class IIa HDACs, increasing the transcription of this deacetylase.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a proposed mechanism based on the experimental data.

claim: Extremely low or undetectable levels of Hdac9 mRNA have been consistently found in C57BL/6 mouse sciatic nerves and cultured rat Schwann cells.
source: However, we have consistently found extremely low or undetectable levels of the mRNA for this protein in the C57BL/6 mouse sciatic nerves and cultured rat Schwann cells (Gomis-Coloma et al., 2018), a result that has been recently confirmed in the Sciatic Nerve ATlas (SNAT, https://www.snat.ethz.ch) (Gerber et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by citations to the authors' previous work and another study.

claim: Hdac9 was among the most robustly upregulated genes by the tKO nerves in the RNA-seq analysis.
source: Surprisingly, we found Hdac9 among the most robustly upregulated genes by the tKO nerves in the RNA-seq analysis (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: The mRNA for Hdac9 was increased by 4.4-fold in the tKO mice (p < 0.0001).
source: As is shown in Figure 9A, the mRNA for Hdac9 was increased by 4.4-fold in the tKO mice (p < 0.0001).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: Hdac9 increase was not found in the dKO and was smaller in the cKO7 (2.4-fold; p = 0.0057) and cKO4 (1.3-fold; p = 0.01) mice.
source: This increase was not found in the dKO and was smaller in the cKO7 (2.4-fold; p = 0.0057) and cKO4 (1.3-fold; p = 0.01) mice.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by RT-qPCR data.

claim: Hdac9 is strongly expressed in the sciatic nerves of the tKO mice to compensate for the absence of other class IIa HDACs.
source: These results suggest that Hdac9 is strongly expressed in the sciatic nerves of the tKO mice to compensate for the absence of other class IIa HDACs.
evidence: This is stated in the results as an interpretation of the RT-qPCR data.

claim: Hdac9 is already induced early in development in the tKO (P2) whereas it was practically undetectable in the nerves of control animals.
source: Indeed, we found that Hdac9 is already induced early in development in the tKO (P2) whereas it was practically undetectable in the nerves of control animals (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 9B.

claim: At P8, Hdac9 expression remains extremely low in control nerves, but it is robustly expressed in the tKO mice (an increase of 5.3-fold; p = 0.0117).
source: At P8, Hdac9 expression remains extremely low in control nerves, but it is robustly expressed in the tKO mice (an increase of 5.3-fold; p = 0.0117), correlating with an increase in the number of myelinated axons (Figure 1B–J).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by RT-qPCR data.

claim: Robust Hdac9 gene expression is maintained in the sciatic nerve of the tKO at P60.
source: Robust Hdac9 gene expression is maintained in the sciatic nerve of the tKO at P60 (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: In the tKO nerves, the lysine 9 of histone three associated to the Hdac9 promoter is more acetylated.
source: Interestingly, we found that in the tKO nerves, the lysine 9 of histone three associated to the Hdac9 promoter is more acetylated (Figure 9C), suggesting that the absence of class IIa HDACs allows the expression of this gene.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 9C.

claim: The absence of class IIa HDACs allows the expression of Hdac9.
source: Interestingly, we found that in the tKO nerves, the lysine 9 of histone three associated to the Hdac9 promoter is more acetylated (Figure 9C), suggesting that the absence of class IIa HDACs allows the expression of this gene.
evidence: This is stated in the results as an interpretation of the ChIP-qPCR data.

claim: Hdac9 gene is further upregulated in the injured sciatic nerves of tKO mice.
source: Importantly, Hdac9 gene is furtherly upregulated in the injured sciatic nerves of tKO mice, as is shown in Figure 9D, where we show the alignment of the reads of the RNA-seq from three individual sciatic nerves from control and tKO mice UI and at 20 dpi, and in Figure 9E, where we followed the mRNA levels of Hdac9 (as Fragments Per Kilobase Million, FPKMs) at 0, 1, 10, and 20 days post crush in the RNA-seq experiment.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 9D and 9E.

claim: In the absence of class IIa Hdacs, repression is lost and Schwann cells start to express de novo Hdac9.
source: Thus far, our data suggested that in the absence of class IIa Hdacs, repression is lost and Schwann cells start to express de novo Hdac9.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: MEF2D regulates the expression of Hdac9 during muscle differentiation and in leiomyosarcoma cells.
source: Interestingly, it has been described that MEF2D binds to the promoter and regulates the expression of Hdac9 during muscle differentiation, and in leiomyosarcoma cells (Di Giorgio et al., 2020; Haberland et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: RNA-seq data showed that Mef2d is upregulated in the sciatic nerves of the tKO mice at 10 and 20 dpi.
source: Also, RNA-seq data showed that Mef2d is upregulated in the sciatic nerves of the tKO mice at 10 and 20 dpi (Figure 9G).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 9G.

claim: Western blot supported the upregulation of Mef2d in tKO nerves.
source: Western blot supported this idea (Figure 9H, I)
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 9H and 9I.

claim: Immunofluorescence studies showed that Mef2d is expressed by Schwann cells (SOX10+).
source: and immunofluorescence studies (Figure 9J) showed that Mef2d is expressed by Schwann cells (SOX10+).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 9J.

claim: MEF2D was detected bound to the promoter of Hdac9 in the tKO nerves at 20 dpi.
source: Importantly, we detected MEF2D bound to the promoter of Hdac9 in the tKO nerves at 20 dpi (Figure 9K).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 9K.

claim: In the tKO nerve, Mef2d is induced to activate the de novo expression of Hdac9 and maintain a sufficient class IIa Hdac gene dose to allow myelin formation during development and after nerve injury.
source: Altogether our data support the view that in the tKO nerve, Mef2d is induced to activate the de novo expression of Hdac9 and maintain a sufficient class IIa Hdac gene dose to allow myelin formation during development and after nerve injury.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Functional redundancies are found in most genomes and are postulated to give robustness to organisms against mutations.
source: Functional redundancies, the consequence of gene duplications, are found in most genomes, and are postulated to give robustness to organisms against mutations.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Redundancies are evolutionarily unstable and have only a transient lifetime.
source: However, it has been also predicted that redundancies are evolutionarily unstable and have only a transient lifetime.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and is based on theoretical predictions in the field.

claim: Numerous examples exist of gene redundancies that have been conserved throughout dilated evolutionary periods.
source: Despite of this, numerous examples exist of gene redundancies that have been conserved throughout dilated evolutionary periods (Kafri et al., 2006; Peng, 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Fluctuations in gene expression (noise) are a well-known phenomenon that has been described from bacteria to mammalian cells.
source: Fluctuations in gene expression (noise) are a well-known phenomenon that has been described from bacteria to mammalian cells, and may have dramatic effects on fitness if they persist long enough (Raser, 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Some gene redundancies have been evolutionarily selected because they can reduce the harmful effects of gene expression noise.
source: It has been suggested that some gene redundancies have been evolutionarily selected because they can reduce the harmful effects of gene expression noise (Kafri et al., 2006).
